name: Curse of knowledge
statement: Once someone knows a thing they cannot set it aside, so they overestimate how much of it other people already know.
meaning: The claim is about a subtraction that people cannot perform. Judging what a less informed person believes means holding your own knowledge out of the calculation, and the finding is that the knowledge leaks back in. Camerer, Loewenstein and Weber wrote the leak down formally. A forecaster with information I1 should report E(X|I0) when asked what someone holding only I0 expects; instead they report a weighted blend of E(X|I0) and E(X|I1), and the weight on their own richer information is the size of the bias. The same structure covers hindsight bias, where the naive perspective being reconstructed is the person's own earlier one, and false-belief reasoning, where it belongs to somebody else.

origin.who: Colin Camerer, George Loewenstein and Martin Weber
origin.note: The paper names the effect and credits the phrase to Robin Hogarth in a footnote. It treats the phenomenon as already established in psychology, citing Fischhoff's 1975 hindsight work, and asks the economic question instead: whether incentives, feedback and markets clear the bias away.

evidence: The economics experiment ran in two stages. In the first, 51 Wharton students read Value Line reports and predicted eight companies' 1980 earnings. In the second, run two months later, groups of nine Wharton students who had traded in earlier market experiments saw the identical reports with the actual 1980 earnings filled in, then traded assets whose dividend was the first group's mean prediction. Pricing the asset correctly required ignoring the true earnings. Equilibrium prices settled between the no-bias and full-bias predictions, and the authors report rejecting both hypotheses strongly. Judgements by Chicago MBA students given incentives (n = 19) or incentives plus feedback (n = 13) showed more bias than judgements made inside the markets, which the paper summarises as the market reducing bias by about half. That reduction reached significance at 5% for three of the eight companies. Feedback on its own did nothing, and the incentives and feedback groups were pooled because their biases did not differ. The famous demonstration is a different study and is described below.

replication.headline: Two large replication efforts disagree. Seven experiments on 3,074 people put the false-belief effect at d = 0.20, which their authors call a failure to replicate. Three later experiments on 1,308 people put it at d = 0.314, and at d = 0.407 for an in-group protagonist.
replication.detail: Birch and Bloom gave 155 students in an introductory psychology course at Yale a displacement task about a girl called Vicki and her violin, and asked for percentage probabilities rather than a yes or no. Knowing where the violin had gone raised ratings for the plausible wrong container from 23% to 34%, t(105) = 2.42, d = 0.472, and lowered ratings for the correct container from 71% to 59%, t(105) = 2.35, d = 0.459. Both comparisons carry prep = .95 in place of a p value. Knowing an implausible location produced no reliable bias, t(97) = 1.44. Ryskin and Brown-Schmidt repeated that experiment seven times, analysing 3,074 people after dropping paper responses whose percentages did not sum to 100, eight in one experiment and 24 in another. Pooling across the seven, the knowledge effect came out at d = 0.20 against the original 0.469, t(1902) = 4.57, p < .001, and the plausibility effect at d = 0.24 against the original 0.645. Those two baselines are their own figures for the original data, which is why 0.469 sits beside the 0.472 printed by Birch and Bloom. Two of the seven runs found the knowledge effect at p < .05, with a third at p = .053. Their own test is that the original design, with about 50 people per condition, had 17% power to detect d = 0.20 and 22% to detect d = 0.24, so the results are substantively different rather than a quiet confirmation. Farrar and Ostojić then ran the task again, recruiting 300, 300 and 780 people on Prolific and analysing 283, 281 and 744 after inclusion criteria, unfinished tasks and suspicion checks. They varied whether the protagonist was an in-group member, an out-group member or a dog. Their meta-analysis of the three put the knowledge effect at d = 0.314, a figure their results section describes as covering all conditions and their discussion as covering the human protagonists. For the in-group protagonist it came out at d = 0.407, rising to d = 0.507 when computed from raw ratings the way Birch and Bloom computed theirs. They read the in-group figure as directly in line with the original. Adding Todd and colleagues' fourth experiment to the pool left the in-group effect at d = 0.428, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.63, and the out-group effect at d = 0.145, 95% CI -0.056 to 0.34, p = 0.16. Their containers differed in shape rather than colour, so these are conceptual replications rather than repeats. What holds up sits elsewhere too. Tullis and Feder had participants study trivia questions and estimate what percentage of novices would know each answer. Across four experiments, when participants had to answer the question themselves first, studying the facts damaged both the calibration and the resolution of those estimates. In the first, on 131 people, calibration was worse in the third round of study than the first, t(130) = 3.21, p = .002, d = 0.28, and resolution fell, t(130) = 3.88, p < .001, d = 0.34. Zhong, Siu and Cheung report six experiments in which paragraphs of related but useless text raised estimates of what peers know, an inflation their abstract calls independent of the classic curse of knowledge.

study.cite: Ryskin, R. A., & Brown-Schmidt, S. (2014). Do adults show a curse of knowledge in false-belief reasoning? A robust estimate of the true effect size. PLoS ONE, 9(3), e92406.

limits: The demonstration everyone quotes was never peer reviewed. Elizabeth Newton's tappers and listeners study is a chapter of her 1990 Stanford doctoral dissertation, UMI order number 9102521, and no journal version of it turned up in Crossref, DataCite, Europe PMC or PubMed. The dissertation was read directly for these figures, and they hold up. 80 Stanford undergraduates were paired, and tappers chose three songs each from a list of 25. Tappers put the chance their listener had named the tune at a mean of 50%, range 10 to 95, SD 25. Listeners scored 3 hits in 120 tries, 2.5%, outside the entire range of the tappers' guesses. The dissertation contradicts itself on that count, giving two of 150 in the abstract and three of 150 in the discussion, against the three of 120 in the results and in the table. The title is also usually got wrong; it is "The rocky road from actions to intentions", not the "Heard and unheard melodies" phrase attached to it in retellings. No replication of the tapping study, in a journal or as a classroom repeat, was located in Crossref, DataCite, Europe PMC, PubMed, PLOS or web search. No effect size is quoted from the economics paper, which reports a bias index rather than a standardised effect. Todd and colleagues' 2011 experiment is closed access on Unpaywall and was not read here, so the pooled figures that include it are taken from Farrar and Ostojić, who worked from its raw data. Zhong, Siu and Cheung's six experiments were reached only through the abstract carried by PubMed and Europe PMC. Guilbault and colleagues' meta-analysis of hindsight bias sits behind a paywall that these checks did not pass. Its pooled estimate was later obtained from the published abstract while writing hindsight bias, entry 48, and is quoted there rather than here. Searches covered Crossref, DataCite, Europe PMC, PubMed, PLOS, Google via web search, and the full text of the six papers held.
misreadings: The tapping figures get quoted as though 50 against 2.5 were the measured size of the curse of knowledge in general. They are one demonstration, in one unpublished study, of a task listeners find close to impossible, and the gap partly measures the difficulty of the task rather than the tappers' egocentrism. Newton's own listeners guessed that only 3% of an audience would name a tune, so the effect is specific to knowing the tune, not a general optimism. The curse is also treated as a fixed trait of experts, where Camerer and colleagues found market experience cut it by about half within a single session. And it is used interchangeably with hindsight bias, entry 48, which is one case of it: the naive perspective being reconstructed there is the judge's own earlier one. The curse of expertise, entry 189, sits under a nearby name and makes a different claim, about how badly experts predict novice performance.
